# The Lawsuits That Could Change Social Media Forever w/ Ben Zipursky

First listed: 2026-06-17 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [Substack: The Lawsuits That Could Change Social Media Forever w/ Ben Zipursky](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/the-lawsuits-that-could-change-social) - 2026-06-17
- [Substack: The Lawsuits That Could Change Social Media Forever w/ Ben Zipursky](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/the-lawsuits-that-could-change-social-ca1) - 2026-06-17

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Benjamin Zipursky separates negligence, consumer fraud, product liability and public nuisance in social-media litigation. He favors ordinary negligence while criticizing expansive nuisance theories and emphasizing federal defenses and appeals. Eisman identifies lasting legal exposure and possible product changes. Later multistate settlements, New Mexico remedies and continuing trials support material risk, but do not establish every causal allegation. The guest misstates the California damages split; Eisman overstates the absence of related appellate precedent and assumes all cases will be appealed. The New Mexico court later rejected direct algorithm redesign while ordering other safeguards and abatement funding.

The central warning about prolonged and potentially substantial exposure has meaningful support. Legal opinions about the proper scope of nuisance are normative, not failed forecasts because a trial judge ruled differently. Preserve the distinction between alleged harm, adjudicated facts, settlement obligations and final appellate outcomes.

## Framework and tools

- Classify cause of action, plaintiff and remedy before assessing exposure.
- Separate third-party publication from a platform's independent design duties.
- Distinguish complaints, jury findings, judgments, settlement and appeals.
- Consider aggregated state exposure rather than only one verdict.
- Separate a normative legal critique from a prediction of judicial outcomes.
- Preserve alternative causes and uncertainty about technical implementation.
- Update legislative pessimism when state activity supplies contrary evidence.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Section 230 statutory text and preemption
- Negligence, strict product liability and consumer-protection claims
- Public-nuisance abatement and injunctive relief
- Compensatory versus punitive damages
- Per-violation civil penalties
- MDL coordination and state-law differences
- First Amendment and Supreme Court review
- Corporate cash flow versus aggregate litigation exposure
